options.explanation: Catalysis is not diagnosed by a straight line.

First order curves rather than running straight.

options.explanation: Blocking is not the mechanism here.

options.text: The temperature fell during the run

questions.stem: For a zero-order reaction the rate equation is

options.text: rate = k, with no concentration term
options.explanation: Zero order removes the reactant from the expression entirely.
That is the first-order rate equation.

questions.stem: State the shape of a zero-order concentration-time graph and what its gradient represents.
questions.modelAnswer: A straight line sloping downwards whose gradient represents the constant rate, equal to k.

questions.stem: State the shapes for first and second order on a concentration-time graph.
questions.modelAnswer: First order: a downward curve that plateaus; second order: a steeper downward curve.

questions.stem: Explain why the zero-order concentration-time graph has a constant gradient.
questions.modelAnswer: The rate of a zero-order reaction does not depend on concentration, so as the reactant is consumed the rate refuses to change; an unchanging rate on a concentration-time plot is exactly an unchanging gradient, a straight line.

questions.stem: A concentration-time graph starts steep and becomes steadily steeper. Which order does this suggest, and which rate equation accompanies it?
questions.modelAnswer: The deepening steepness marks second order, and the accompanying rate equation is rate = k[A]^2.

questions.stem: A reaction shows successive half-lives of 100 s, 50 s and 25 s. The order is

options.explanation: No fractional evidence appears here.

options.text: Zero order, whose half-lives decrease with time
options.explanation: Halving takes less and less time as the reaction progresses.

options.text: First order, whose half-lives are constant
options.explanation: First-order half-lives would all read 100 s.
Second-order half-lives grow, not shrink.

questions.stem: The trademark of a first-order reaction is

options.text: A half-life that shortens as the reaction runs
options.explanation: That is the zero-order signature.

options.text: A half-life that changes with volume
options.explanation: Half-life is a time, unaffected by vessel size.

options.text: A half-life that remains constant throughout the reaction
options.explanation: Each successive halving takes the same time.

options.text: A half-life that lengthens as the reaction runs
options.explanation: That is the second-order signature.

questions.stem: For a second-order reaction, as the reaction progresses the half-life

options.explanation: Decreasing half-lives mark zero order.
Constant half-lives mark first order.
No alternating pattern exists.

options.text: Increases, because the falling concentration slows the rate ever more
options.explanation: Rate tied to the square of a shrinking concentration makes halvings slower.

questions.stem: The half-life method identifies order because

options.text: Each order couples rate to concentration differently, giving a characteristic pattern of successive halvings
options.explanation: The halving pattern is the order's fingerprint.

options.text: Half-life equals the rate constant for every order
options.explanation: Only under special relations is that true.
The whole method rests on order dependence.
Energy has no role here.

questions.stem: A concentration-time curve shows the concentration halving every 40 seconds without exception. The rate equation is

options.explanation: The half-life table already decides the order.
A constant half-life is the first-order signature.
Zero order would show shrinking half-lives.
Second order would show stretching half-lives.

questions.stem: State what happens to successive half-lives in a zero-order reaction.
questions.modelAnswer: The successive half-lives decrease, taking less time for each halving as the reaction progresses.

questions.stem: State the half-life pattern of a first-order reaction.
questions.modelAnswer: The half-life remains constant throughout the reaction, each halving taking the same time.

questions.stem: Explain why a constant half-life indicates first order.
questions.modelAnswer: First-order rate tracks concentration, so each halving of the concentration halves the rate as well, and the time the next halving needs repeats identically - a signature unique to proportionality.

questions.stem: A reactant's concentration falls from 2.0 to 1.0 mol dm^-3 in 30 s, then from 1.0 to 0.5 mol dm^-3 in 60 s. Deduce the order.
questions.modelAnswer: The halving time stretched from 30 s to 60 s, so successive half-lives increase and the reaction is second order.

questions.stem: State the rate-concentration shape for a first-order reaction.
questions.modelAnswer: A straight line through the origin, reflecting rate = k[A].

questions.stem: State the three rate-concentration shapes in order words.
questions.modelAnswer: Zero order: horizontal line; first order: straight line through the origin; second order: upward curve.

questions.stem: Explain why the first-order rate-concentration graph passes through the origin.
questions.modelAnswer: With rate = k[A], setting the concentration to zero leaves a rate of zero, so the line must start at the origin and rise proportionally.

questions.stem: A rate-concentration graph is a curve through the origin and the matching concentration-time graph shows increasing half-lives. Deduce the order and the rate equation.
questions.modelAnswer: The curved rate plot and the stretching half-lives both point to second order, so the rate equation is rate = k[A]^2.
